title: Week 119 · Lesson 143: Falls, Gait, Balance & Mobility — FNP-Level Risk Evaluation and Prevention
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 119 — Lesson 143: Falls, Gait, Balance & Mobility

FNP-level goal: Treat every fall as a clinical event with a mechanism, injury risk, and preventable contributors; distinguish a simple trip from syncope, seizure, neurologic disease, medication toxicity, or acute illness; perform a focused gait and fall-risk assessment; and build an individualized plan that preserves mobility rather than increasing fear and inactivity.

Learning Objectives

  • Screen older adults for falls, unsteadiness, and fear of falling, then determine who needs a multifactorial assessment.
  • Reconstruct the event and distinguish environmental falls from syncope, seizure, neurologic emergencies, and medication-related instability.
  • Perform focused orthostatic, cardiovascular, neurologic, musculoskeletal, vision, foot, gait, and balance evaluation.
  • Identify head injury, fracture, spinal injury, stroke, arrhythmia, and other red flags requiring urgent or emergency care.
  • Implement evidence-based exercise, medication, vision, footwear, assistive-device, home-safety, bone-health, and follow-up interventions.

Part 1 — A Fall Is a Symptom, Not a Diagnosis

Falls are not an inevitable part of aging. They may be the first sign of acute illness, orthostatic hypotension, arrhythmia, neuropathy, parkinsonism, vision loss, medication toxicity, weakness, unsafe footwear, or environmental hazard. Most falls are multifactorial: several modest risks become dangerous when physiologic reserve is limited.

Do not label an unwitnessed fall as mechanical until the event has been reconstructed. A patient may say they tripped because they do not remember losing consciousness. The FNP must identify injury, mechanism, modifiable risk, and the correct disposition.

Part 2 — Screen Routinely and After Every Fall

Ask at least annually and whenever a patient presents after a fall: Have you fallen in the past year? Do you feel unsteady when standing or walking? Are you worried about falling? A positive answer, observed gait difficulty, or clinician concern should trigger further assessment.

Ask how many falls occurred, whether any caused injury, whether the patient needed help to rise, and whether activity has been restricted afterward. A single fall with loss of consciousness or serious injury may be more concerning than several clearly explained low-risk stumbles.

Part 3 — Reconstruct the Event

Clarify where, when, and during what activity the fall occurred. Ask about position before the event, turning, toileting, stairs, lighting, footwear, assistive device, obstacles, alcohol, meals, hydration, recent illness, and timing of medicines. Determine the direction of the fall and what body part struck the ground.

Ask about preceding dizziness, spinning, palpitations, chest discomfort, dyspnea, weakness, numbness, visual change, headache, nausea, sweating, or an urgent need to void. Ask about loss of consciousness, memory gap, witnessed movements, tongue injury, incontinence, confusion, and speed of recovery. Collateral history may be essential.

Part 4 — Mechanical Fall, Syncope, or Seizure?

A clear trip over an obstacle with full recall and immediate recovery supports an environmental mechanism, but does not exclude weakness, poor vision, or unsafe gait. Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion and usually has rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous recovery. Orthostatic, reflex, structural cardiac, and arrhythmic causes require different urgency.

Seizure is more likely with a stereotyped aura, prolonged tonic-clonic activity, lateral tongue injury, prolonged post-event confusion, or known epilepsy, although none is perfect. Myoclonic movements can occur during syncope. New focal deficit, persistent altered mental status, severe headache, or inability to provide a coherent history requires urgent neurologic evaluation.

Part 5 — Immediate Injury Survey

Before long-term prevention, evaluate trauma. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, head and cervical injury, focal tenderness, deformity, limb length and rotation, weight-bearing, range of motion, skin injury, and neurovascular status. Older adults may have major fracture with modest swelling or pain.

Suspect hip fracture with groin or hip pain, inability to bear weight, shortened externally rotated leg, or pain with gentle movement. Occult fracture is possible even when initial radiographs are unrevealing. Persistent inability to bear weight or focal pain needs advanced evaluation rather than reassurance.

Part 6 — Head Trauma and Antithrombotic Therapy

Ask specifically about head strike, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, bleeding disorder, alcohol, vomiting, headache, amnesia, behavior change, and neurologic symptoms. Intracranial bleeding may present subtly or be delayed in an older adult.

Loss of consciousness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, focal deficit, seizure, confusion, significant mechanism, or anticoagulant-associated head injury requires urgent emergency assessment according to current head-injury protocols. Do not use a normal brief office examination to dismiss evolving intracranial injury.

Part 7 — Focused Vital Signs and Orthostatic Blood Pressure

Measure pulse, rhythm, oxygen saturation, temperature, and blood pressure. For orthostatic testing, allow the patient to rest supine, obtain blood pressure and heart rate, then repeat after standing at clinically appropriate intervals, commonly within one and three minutes, while observing symptoms and safety.

A sustained fall of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within three minutes supports orthostatic hypotension, but symptoms and context matter. A blunted heart-rate response may suggest autonomic dysfunction or rate-limiting medication; marked tachycardia may suggest volume depletion. Severe symptoms, hypotension, ischemia, or inability to stand safely changes disposition.

Part 8 — Cardiovascular Causes

Ask about exertional syncope, palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, known structural disease, heart failure, family history of sudden death, and medications that slow rate or lower pressure. Examine rhythm, murmurs, volume status, pulses, and signs of heart failure. Obtain an ECG when syncope, arrhythmia, conduction disease, or cardiac cause is possible.

Syncope during exertion, while supine, without warning, or with abnormal ECG, significant murmur, chest pain, heart failure, or family history is high risk. Aortic stenosis, bradyarrhythmia, ventricular tachyarrhythmia, pulmonary embolism, myocardial ischemia, and major hemorrhage are not outpatient fall-prevention problems.

Part 9 — Neurologic and Vestibular Contributors

Assess cranial nerves, strength, tone, coordination, sensation, reflexes when indicated, pronator drift, speech, cognition, and gait. Parkinsonian gait may show reduced arm swing, shuffling, rigidity, freezing, and difficulty turning. Cerebellar disease may cause wide-based gait and truncal instability. Peripheral neuropathy reduces distal sensation and proprioception, especially in low light.

Vertigo requires a syndrome-based assessment. Do not perform positional maneuvers in an unstable patient or assume all dizziness is benign. New focal deficit, inability to walk, severe headache, central eye findings, or acute continuous vestibular symptoms with stroke risk requires emergency stroke evaluation.

Part 10 — Musculoskeletal, Foot, and Pain Assessment

Examine lower-extremity strength, joint range, pain, deformity, leg length, spine, and feet. Osteoarthritis pain, hip abductor weakness, ankle limitation, foot deformity, callus, ulcer, and poorly fitting shoes can change gait. Ask about numbness and whether the patient feels the floor.

Pain can reduce activity and strength, but analgesic treatment may add sedation or orthostasis. Pair pain management with function goals, physical therapy, footwear, and medication review rather than adding sedatives to a mobility problem.

Part 11 — Observe Gait, Do Not Only Ask About It

Watch the patient rise, stand, initiate walking, turn, stop, and sit. Note use of arms, step length, foot clearance, symmetry, base width, speed, sway, freezing, pain, and device use. Observe with the usual footwear and assistive device.

Validated tools such as the Timed Up and Go, 30-Second Chair Stand, and staged balance tests can identify impairment and track change. A cutoff is not a diagnosis and should not replace clinical reasoning. A patient who appears unsafe should be guarded and should not be forced through a test for documentation.

Part 12 — Timed Up and Go

The Timed Up and Go asks the patient to rise from a chair, walk a short marked distance, turn, return, and sit. Observe technique as well as time: pushing heavily with the arms, hesitation, wide turn, poor foot clearance, grabbing furniture, and uncontrolled sitting reveal actionable problems.

Interpret performance in context of age, height, cognition, pain, device, environment, and baseline. Use the test to guide intervention and referral, not to certify that a patient cannot fall.

Part 13 — Medication Review Is Essential

Connect Lesson 142 directly to falls. Review benzodiazepines, hypnotics, opioids, anticholinergics, antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihypertensives, diuretics, glucose-lowering medicines, anticonvulsants, muscle relaxants, and alcohol or cannabis. Ask what was started, increased, stopped, or taken as needed before the event.

Deprescribe or adjust through indication-based shared decisions and taper dependence-producing drugs safely. Do not replace one sedative with another. Check renal function, volume status, hypoglycemia, and drug combinations. Collaborate with pharmacists and prescribers so the patient receives one coherent plan.

Part 14 — Vision, Hearing, and Multifocal Lenses

Assess visual acuity, cataract or retinal history, glaucoma care, depth perception concern, and whether glasses are current. Sudden visual loss, painful red eye, or neurologic visual deficit needs urgent evaluation. Hearing loss may impair environmental awareness and communication during mobility training.

New multifocal or bifocal lenses can distort depth on stairs or uneven ground. Do not advise patients to abandon necessary correction without assessment; coordinate eye care and teach safe adaptation. Improve lighting and contrast in the home.

Part 15 — Toileting, Nocturia, and Night Falls

Urgency, incontinence, constipation, diuretics, poor sleep, and dark routes to the bathroom create a common risk cluster. Ask whether falls occur while rushing at night and whether the patient avoids mobility aids indoors.

Address the urinary cause, medication timing when appropriate, bedside lighting, clear pathways, footwear, and safe toileting supports. Avoid reflex anticholinergic prescribing without considering cognition, retention, and fall burden.

Part 16 — Exercise Is a Core Intervention

For community-dwelling adults at increased fall risk, current USPSTF guidance recommends exercise interventions. Effective programs commonly include gait, balance, functional, and strength or resistance training, with progression and sufficient challenge. Walking alone may improve health but may not correct balance and strength deficits.

Refer to physical therapy or a qualified community program when needed. Match intensity to cardiac, neurologic, musculoskeletal, and cognitive status. Teach that supervised activity builds reserve; excessive restriction causes deconditioning and may increase future risk.

Part 17 — Individualized Multifactorial Intervention

A multifactorial plan targets risks actually found: medication reduction, orthostatic management, strength and balance training, vision care, foot and footwear treatment, assistive-device fitting, home modification, continence care, nutrition, and chronic disease management. Offering every intervention to everyone is less useful than closing the loop on identified risks.

The USPSTF recommends individualizing multifactorial interventions because benefit depends on prior falls, comorbidities, preferences, feasibility, and the specific modifiable factors present.

Part 18 — Home Safety and Occupational Therapy

Ask about stairs, rails, rugs, cords, clutter, pets, bathroom surfaces, lighting, furniture height, and access to frequently used items. A checklist is helpful, but a home assessment by occupational therapy may reveal hazards the clinic cannot see and can match modifications to the patient's actual function.

Useful changes may include grab bars, improved lighting, secure railings, removal of loose hazards, nonslip surfaces, reachable storage, and safer seating. Do not make the home so restrictive that independence and meaningful activity disappear.

Part 19 — Canes, Walkers, and Device Fit

An assistive device helps only when selected, fitted, and used correctly. A cane on the wrong side, a walker set too high, worn tips, inaccessible brakes, or leaving the device across the room can increase risk. Observe actual use, including turns, thresholds, stairs, and transfers.

Physical or occupational therapy can select and train the device. Ask whether the patient avoids it because of stigma, weight, transport difficulty, cognition, or poor fit, then solve the real barrier.

Part 20 — Bone Health and Injury Prevention

Fall prevention and fracture prevention are related but distinct. Review osteoporosis screening, prior fragility fracture, calcium and vitamin D adequacy, tobacco, alcohol, weight, glucocorticoid exposure, and treatment adherence. A minor fall can cause major injury when bone strength is low.

Hip-protection strategies, safe transfer training, and osteoporosis treatment may be relevant in high-risk settings. Do not rely on vitamin supplementation alone as a complete fall-prevention program.

Part 21 — Fear of Falling and the Deconditioning Cycle

Fear after a fall can produce activity restriction, isolation, weakness, worse balance, and another fall. Ask what the patient stopped doing and whether confidence, mood, or social participation changed. Validate the fear without endorsing permanent immobility.

Use graded, supervised activity, realistic safety planning, behavioral support, and measurable function goals such as walking to the mailbox or transferring independently. Success is not only fewer falls; it is safer participation in valued life.

Part 22 — Nutrition, Sarcopenia, and Frailty

Weight loss, inadequate protein or calories, vitamin deficiency, oral disease, dysphagia, and social isolation can worsen weakness. Review appetite, weight trajectory, access to food, dentition, swallowing, and the ability to shop and cook.

Exercise and nutrition plans should be coordinated. Supplements do not replace assessment of disease, food insecurity, or swallowing risk. Frailty increases vulnerability but also identifies opportunities for strength, function, and support interventions.

Part 23 — When Testing Helps

Testing should answer a clinical question. Depending on the story, consider ECG, glucose, blood count, electrolytes, kidney function, thyroid testing, medication levels, cardiac monitoring, echocardiography, neurologic imaging, vestibular evaluation, or injury imaging. Routine broad panels without a hypothesis may create noise.

Recurrent unexplained falls may be occult syncope. A normal office ECG does not exclude intermittent arrhythmia. Choose monitoring duration and specialty referral based on event frequency, cardiac risk, and associated features.

Part 24 — Follow-Up Is Part of the Intervention

Document the fall mechanism, injuries, risk factors, interventions, who owns referrals, and when results will be reviewed. Reassess falls, near-falls, fear, orthostatic symptoms, gait, medication changes, and exercise adherence. Confirm that PT, eye care, home safety, and device plans actually occurred.

Provide a written emergency plan and teach the patient how to rise safely only if uninjured, how to call for help, and why a wearable alert or regular check-in may be useful. A referral without follow-through is not completed prevention.

Part 25 — Red Flags and Disposition

Emergency evaluation is required for suspected hip or spinal fracture, inability to bear weight after significant trauma, head injury with high-risk features, new focal neurologic deficit, persistent altered mental status, seizure, exertional or supine syncope, chest pain, severe dyspnea, major bleeding, unstable arrhythmia, or shock.

Expedited evaluation is appropriate for recurrent unexplained falls, symptomatic orthostasis, progressive gait disorder, new parkinsonism, foot drop, rapid functional decline, unsafe living situation, or inability to use essential mobility aids. Stable patients still need a time-bound prevention and follow-up plan.

Clinical Case 1 — The Fall on Anticoagulation

An 81-year-old taking apixaban falls on stairs, strikes the head, and initially says they feel fine. The spouse reports a brief memory gap and a worsening headache. The FNP does not perform routine fall counseling first; the patient is sent for emergency head-injury assessment because delayed intracranial bleeding is possible.

Clinical Case 2 — Nighttime Orthostasis

A 79-year-old falls twice when rushing to the bathroom after several days of poor intake. Supine-to-standing blood pressure falls with dizziness; the regimen includes a diuretic, multiple antihypertensives, and a sedating sleep medicine. The FNP assesses volume depletion and acute illness, reviews doses and timing, addresses nocturia and lighting, and creates a monitored medication and hydration plan rather than labeling the falls clumsiness.

Clinical Case 3 — The Shuffling Gait

A 76-year-old has near-falls, slower turns, reduced arm swing, short steps, and occasional freezing. The FNP recognizes a progressive neurologic gait pattern, reviews dopamine-blocking medicines and cognition, evaluates injury risk, refers for neurologic and physical therapy assessment, and introduces a properly fitted device without delaying the diagnostic workup.

FNP High-Yield Framework: FALL SAFE

  1. F — Find the event: timing, position, trigger, prodrome, consciousness, witness, recovery.
  2. A — Assess acute danger: head, hip, spine, stroke, seizure, bleeding, cardiac instability.
  3. L — Look at the whole patient: orthostatics, rhythm, neurologic status, strength, feet, vision, cognition.
  4. L — List contributors: medicines, illness, hydration, environment, footwear, toileting, substances.
  5. S — See the gait: rise, walk, turn, sit, device use, validated functional measures.
  6. A — Act on modifiable risks: exercise, medication, vision, home, device, continence, nutrition.
  7. F — Fortify against injury: bone health, emergency response, safe transfers, caregiver education.
  8. E — Ensure follow-up: referral completion, repeat symptoms, near-falls, function, and closed loops.

Take-Home Summary

A fall is a diagnostic clue and a prevention opportunity. FNP-level care first protects the patient from missed trauma, stroke, seizure, syncope, and medication toxicity; then reconstructs the event and examines gait, balance, blood pressure, heart, nervous system, strength, feet, vision, and environment. Exercise-based and individualized interventions should preserve confident mobility rather than create fear-driven inactivity.

Educational note: Apply current CDC STEADI, USPSTF fall-prevention, NIA fall and fracture, trauma, syncope, and local emergency guidance. Head injury with high-risk features, suspected fracture, new neurologic deficit, seizure, exertional or supine syncope, chest pain, severe dyspnea, major bleeding, or hemodynamic instability requires emergency evaluation.
